problem: MLLMs such as GPT-4V/O still struggle with 3D spatial and long-video temporal reasoning, and prior fixes need specialized architectures, 3D inputs or task-specific fine-tuning, treating space and time separately.
motivation: Spatial-temporal reasoning is a bottleneck for deploying MLLMs in real-world and embodied settings. Classical vision shows that correspondences across views/frames are key to 3D understanding, yet MLLMs are not given them explicitly, so a cheap way to supply correspondences could help both space and time.
key_idea: Run an off-the-shelf video tracker to get instance-level correspondences across sparsely sampled frames, and overlay the few most prominent instance IDs as numeric markers on the images before feeding them to the MLLM (training-free visual prompting).
insight: Correspondence information alone, even coarse and imperfect, lets MLLMs build a consistent spatial-temporal model from 2D frames. Ablations on ScanQA (GPT-4V) show that overlaying all dense correspondences or oversized marks and masks hurts through occlusion, while a handful of moderately sized markers (optionally with outlines) works best. A diagnostic benchmark shows CC removes camera-motion bias: forward/reverse accuracy of GPT-4o is 58.0/50.4 without CC, and 71.2/71.2 with CC.
method: Tracking correspondences: run an off-the-shelf video tracker (Track Anything; SAMv2 for navigation) to get class-agnostic instance segmentation masks with consistent IDs over all frames.
Sparsify frames: run tracking on the high-frame-rate sequence, then uniformly keep only m<<n frames and their masks to cut MLLM cost.
Select coarse correspondences: rank instance IDs by frequency of occurrence across retained frames (ties broken by summed area) and keep the top-K as tracklets.
Visualize: draw a fixed-size red circle marker with white ID text at the mask centroid of each selected instance in each retained frame (segmentation outlines optional).
Navigation use: online, SAMv2 labels each new observation using the episodic history; GPT-4o outputs FORWARD(distance)/TURN-LEFT/TURN-RIGHT(angle)/STOP with NavGPT-style prompts.
Open models: fine-tune LLaVA on ~1.2M image/video samples where CC is applied only to ScanQA data, then use CC at inference (or only in training as augmentation).

setting.backbone: GPT-4V / GPT-4o (frozen, prompted); LLaVA (fine-tuned) for the open-model experiments
setting.training_data: none (training-free) for GPT models; LLaVA fine-tuned on ~1.2M image/video samples with ScanQA as the only 3D data
setting.observation: monocular RGB frames (sparsified, 4-8 frames for QA; one image per step for navigation) with tracking-based marker overlays

numbers_note: Only one navigation result, on a 100-episode subset; the paper calls the benchmark 'R2R' in VLN-CE. The other benchmarks (ScanQA, OpenEQA, EgoSchema, SQA3D) are not navigation benchmarks and are not listed.
results: CC lifts GPT-4o on R2R (VLN-CE, 100 episodes) from SR 12.0 to 23.0 and SPL 10.37 to 21.03. It also improves GPT-4o on ScanQA (CIDEr 72.2 to 87.0), OpenEQA EM-EQA (49.4 to 59.1) and EgoSchema (67.2 to 73.2, above LangRepo at 66.2), and LLaVA on ScanQA and SQA3D.
limitations: Navigation evaluated only on a 100-episode subset with absolute performance still low (SR 23%) and no comparison to dedicated VLN methods.
Depends on the quality of off-the-shelf trackers, and marker size, shape and count need tuning (ablated only on ScanQA with GPT-4V).
Open-source models need fine-tuning to read markers and handle multiple images; the open-model study covers only 3D QA.
